C3.title: IL-17 aggravates the neuroinflammatory response in depression by regulating microglial polarization through the JAK1/STAT3 signaling pathway
C3.abstract: Background: Microglia-mediated neuroinflammation is closely related to the development of depression. As a proinflammatory cytokine, IL-17 plays a key role in various neuroinflammatory diseases. This study aimed to investigate the potential molecular mechanisms through which IL-17 affects neuroinflammation in depression through the regulation of microglial polarization. Methods: A chronic unpredictable mild stress (CUMS)-induced mouse model of depression and an LPS-treated BV2 cell model were used. The depression-like behavior of the mice was evaluated using the sucrose preference test (SPT), tail suspension test (TST), and forced swim test (FST). Neuronal injury was assessed using HE staining. The levels of neurotransmitters and inflammatory cytokines were analyzed using ELISA. Microglial polarization was analyzed by flow cytometry and immunofluorescence, and the expression of IL-17A and JAK1/STAT3 pathway-related proteins was assessed using Western blotting. Results: IL-17 was highly expressed in clinical specimens from patients with depression, mice treated with CUMS and BV2 cells. The inhibition of IL-17 improved depression-like behavior in CUMS-treated mice, reduced neuronal damage, and increased the expression of the neurotransmitters 5-HT, NE, and DA. In addition, IL-17 inhibition inhibited M1 microglial polarization and inflammation. In terms of molecular mechanisms, IL-17 promoted microglial M1 polarization by activating the JAK1/STAT3 signaling pathway and aggravating neuroinflammation related to depression. The use of the JAK/STAT pathway activator RO8191 attenuated the inhibitory effect of IL-17 inhibition on microglial M1 polarization. Conclusion: IL-17 activates JAK1/STAT3 signaling, promotes M1 microglial polarization, and aggravates neuroinflammation related to depression.

C3.title: Beyond monoamines: a multi-systems molecular framework for major depressive disorder
C3.abstract: For over five decades, the monoamine hypothesis has anchored the conceptual and pharmacological approach to major depressive disorder (MDD), yet nearly one-third of patients fail to achieve remission with standard antidepressants, and therapeutic response is delayed by weeks. This narrative review offers a critical synthesis of recent high-impact literature drawn on evidence from genomic, molecular, and translational studies across six domains: genomic architecture, epigenetic dysregulation, neuroinflammation, neurotrophic signalling, gut-brain axis, and rapid-acting antidepressant mechanisms, to construct a multi-systems framework of MDD pathophysiology and, as a secondary and explicitly scoped aim, to identify translational priorities for South Asian, particularly Indian, populations; the evidence reviewed is global in scope. A 2025 genome-wide association study (GWAS) of 688,808 cases identified 697 independent associations mapping to 635 genomic risk loci implicating glutamatergic, GABAergic, and neuropeptidergic systems. Environmental stressors converge on this genetic susceptibility through DNA methylation, histone modification, and non-coding RNA-mediated epigenetic reprogramming. An inflammatory MDD subgroup, characterised by kynurenine pathway disruption and microglial dysregulation, is of interest for patient stratification. Rapid-acting antidepressants proposed to act through TrkB-BDNF-dependent synaptic plasticity offer a mechanistic account of their fast onset, although the direct-binding theory awaits independent replication. Gut microbiome dysbiosis, particularly among neurotransmitter-producing taxa, further extends the pathophysiological map beyond the brain itself. Together, these findings support a shift from a unidimensional monoaminergic model to an integrated, multi-systems molecular framework of MDD. Realising the clinical potential of this framework will require validated precision biomarker panels, dedicated South Asian GWAS cohorts, and longitudinal multi-omics studies.

C3.title: Oviductus Ranae Protein Hydrolysate (ORPH) Ameliorates CUMS-Induced Depressive-Like Behaviors in Mice via Modulation of Gut Microbiota and Metabolic Signatures: An Integrated Multi-Omics Investigation
C3.abstract: Depression constitutes a significant global health burden, manifesting as persistent low mood, anhedonia, and behavioral disturbances. The pathogenesis of depression is multifactorial, involving hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis dysregulation, monoaminergic neurotransmitter abnormalities, and neuroinflammatory processes. Oviductus Ranae protein hydrolysate (ORPH) is an enzymatically hydrolysed extract derived from the dried oviducts of female Rana dybowskii Günther (Oviductus Ranae, OR). This esteemed traditional Chinese medicine, indigenous to Northeast China, has been utilized as a valuable tonic for centuries. Previous in vivo investigations have demonstrated the anti-neuroinflammatory effects of OR. Chronic unpredictable mild stress (CUMS) is widely used to establish a mouse model of depressive-like phenotypes. This study aimed to investigate whether ORPH could alleviate CUMS-induced depressive-like behaviors in mice and explore its underlying mechanisms from the perspective of gut microbiota and metabolic profiles. A CUMS paradigm was employed to establish a murine model of depression, and the effects of 0.2, 0.4, or 0.8 g/kg ORPH on depressive-like behaviors were systematically evaluated. Biochemical analyses were conducted to quantify inflammatory mediators, neurotransmitters, and HPA axis-associated hormones in murine serum and brain tissue. Multi-omics approaches, encompassing brain tissue metabolomics, fecal metabolomics, and gut microbiota sequencing, were utilized to elucidate key metabolic constituents and signaling pathways implicated in the regulation of cerebral and gut microbial communities. In vivo experiments were conducted to investigate the effects of microbiota depletion and blockade of key metabolites on the therapeutic efficacy of ORPH. Administration of ORPH at doses of 0.2, 0.4, or 0.8 g/kg markedly ameliorated depressive-like behaviors in CUMS-exposed mice. ORPH increased the sucrose preference rate, reduced immobility time in the FST and TST, and shortened the escape latency in the MWM of CUMS mice. Biochemical assays revealed that ORPH attenuated serum and cerebral concentrations of pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, IL-1β, and TNF-α), reduced circulating ACTH and CRH levels, decreased cerebral CORT content, and elevated cerebral 5-HT and NE levels. Moreover, ORPH significantly mitigated hippocampal tissue injury and apoptosis. Metabolomic analyses identified therapeutic modulation of pathways such as sphingolipid and tryptophan metabolism, while gut microbiota profiling highlighted the enrichment of these taxa, including Lactobacillus. The protective effect of ORPH was obviously weakened after microbiota depletion, and similar attenuation was observed upon inhibiting tryptophan hydroxylase (TPH) activity and sphingosine kinase (SphK). These findings indicate that ORPH may exert favorable therapeutic potential against CUMS-induced depressive-like phenotypes, possibly through modulation of dysregulated sphingolipid and tryptophan metabolism, which could contribute to the alleviation of neuroinflammation linked to gut microbiota dysbiosis.

D1.title: Semantic Processing in Unresponsive Patients With Acute Brain Injury
D1.abstract: Early prognostication after acute brain injury (ABI) is challenging because behavioral responsiveness may not accurately reflect preserved cognitive function. Neural responses to semantic incongruity can identify language processing despite the absence of overt behavior. We investigated whether bedside EEG could detect semantic processing in unresponsive patients with ABI and whether its presence was associated with long-term outcomes. In this prospective 2-center cohort study, unresponsive adults with ABI admitted to neurologic intensive care units between 2022 and 2025 underwent bedside EEG during a language paradigm comparing congruent and incongruent sentence endings (e.g., "my favorite color is green/soon"). Semantic processing was defined by differential event-related responses within centroparietal channels (300-500 milliseconds) using cluster-based permutation testing with false discovery rate correction. Outcomes were assessed for recovery of consciousness and functional recovery (Glasgow Outcome Scale-Extended score ≥4) at 12 months by blinded interviewers. Diagnostic performance was evaluated using sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, accuracy, and likelihood ratios. D1.title: System-level nonequivalence between integrated information and expected free energy in noisy permutation networks

D1.title: Common phenomenal and neural substrate geometry in visual motion perception
D1.abstract: What is a possible physical substrate of the qualitative aspects of consciousness (qualia)? Answering this question is a central goal of consciousness research. Due to their subjective and ineffable nature, finding a quantitative way to characterise qualia from verbal description has thus far proven elusive. Yet, as far as we know, no attempts have been made to evaluate the relationship between a certain structure of qualia and the structure of a candidate underlying physical substrate. From human participants (N=171), we obtained dissimilarity ratings of visual motion experiences induced by 48 stimuli, spanning 8 directions and 6 spatial frequencies. D1.title: From Quantum Brain to Quantum Mind: The Ontological Promotion Gap in Quantum-Biological Theories of Consciousness
D1.abstract: Quantum effects in biological systems are increasingly investigated at molecular, cellular, and neural scales, yet evidence for quantum organization in a living brain does not by itself determine the ontological status of the conscious states realized by that brain. This article distinguishes seven claims often compressed under "quantum consciousness": quantum occurrence, causal relevance, constitutive relevance, phenomenal bridging, phenomenal individuation, quantum mental status, and quantum-formal adequacy. It argues that evidence for the first three-even if decisive-does not by itself establish quantum mental status. I call this cross-level inferential discontinuity the Ontological Promotion Gap. The argument is developed in relation to current quantum-biological approaches to consciousness, including hierarchical microtubule models, nuclear-spin mechanisms, non-classical neuroimaging, dissipative quantum-brain models, autopoietic quantum constraints, and quantum-like cognition. Drawing on multilevel biological organization and contemporary neurophenomenology, the paper introduces a Phenomenal Individuation Condition: for a conscious state to be non-trivially quantum, quantum-specific structure must contribute to the organization or counterfactual differentiation of the phenomenal state itself, rather than merely occur within its biological realization. Quantum-like cognition supplies the converse dissociation: quantum formalism can characterize cognition without establishing quantum physical implementation. The resulting framework yields a Level-Specific Quantum Attribution Principle and an explicit experimental decision structure for determining what different classes of quantum-biological evidence do-and do not-license us to conclude about a quantum mind.

D1.title: Formalizing consciousness: a comparative mathematical analysis of leading theories
D1.abstract: This article provides a unified and accessible exposition of major mathematically articulated frameworks for consciousness: Integrated Information Theory (IIT), Global Workspace Theory (GWT), Active Inference (AIF), higher-order representation (HOR) approaches, and the Projective Consciousness Model (PCM). Building on probability theory, information theory, and geometric structures, we reformulate their core mechanisms in a shared mathematical language at the computational and algorithmic levels, following Marr's hierarchy. This enables rigorous comparison across theories that are often treated as conceptually incommensurable. Our analysis identifies shared formal tools, differences in explanatory scope, and specific questions for computational comparison. GWT emphasizes global availability; IIT emphasizes irreducible causal integration; Active Inference and HOR emphasize hierarchical inference and conscious access under uncertainty; PCM emphasizes the perspectival geometry of conscious experience. We assess computational tractability across frameworks and show that some apparent disagreements reflect differences in explanatory level rather than direct theoretical contradiction. We use this unified formal treatment to outline a route toward future computational comparisons: common testbed models in which integration, broadcasting, higher-order access, and perspectival transformations can be studied within the same agent architecture. The goal is to make overlaps, divergences, and empirical commitments across theories more explicit, thereby supporting more systematic model comparison in consciousness science.

D2.title: Protocol for measuring the effects of cortical scotoma on visual space perception

D3.abstract: Aeromedical certification is based on a safety-first principle: a pilot or other aircrew member must not have a medical disorder that creates an unacceptable risk of sudden or subtle incapacitation during flight. Cardiovascular disease remains one of the most important determinants of flight fitness, as it may impair consciousness, judgment, rhythm stability, exercise capacity, and hemodynamic reserve. Modern aeromedical decision-making therefore requires the integration of aviation law, operational risk, contemporary cardiology guidelines, advanced imaging, biomarkers, and long-term surveillance. The International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) Annex 1 provides the global licensing framework; the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) Part-MED, together with its Acceptable Means of Compliance and Guidance Material, defines detailed operational standards in Europe; and the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) employs a protocol- and special issuance-based system for many cardiovascular and metabolic disorders. This review summarizes the aeromedical assessment of hypertension, diabetes mellitus, chronic and acute coronary syndromes, heart failure, cardiomy-opathies, arrhythmias and conduction disorders, pacemakers and implantable cardiac devices, valvular heart disease, aortic disease, congenital heart disease, venous throm-boembolism, cardiovascular pharmacotherapy, and major respiratory conditions rel-evant to flight certification. The manuscript is aligned with current European Society of Cardiology cardiovascular guidance and with the operational aeromedical principles applied by ICAO, EASA, FAA, and the Turkish Directorate General of Civil Aviation. In general, preserved ventricular function, absence of significant symptoms, low thrombo-embolic and arrhythmic risk, stable treatment, and adequate exercise capacity support certification or restricted certification. In contrast, uncontrolled hypertension, unstable diabetes, significant residual myocardial ischemia, reduced ejection fraction, malignant ventricular arrhythmias, implantable defibrillator therapy, severe valvular disease, significant aortic pathology, major congenital hemodynamic lesions, or poorly controlled sleep apnea usually preclude certification. Final decisions remain individualized and depend on license class, operational role, treatment burden, surveillance data, and the judgment of the aeromedical authority.

D3.title: Transient neurological deterioration after patent foramen ovale closure associated with nitrous oxide exposure in an adolescent with homozygous MTHFR polymorphism
D3.abstract: Transient ischaemic attack after patent foramen ovale closure presents diagnostic challenges. A 17-year-old male with homozygous MTHFR polymorphism underwent successful patent foramen ovale closure under nitrous oxide anaesthesia. Post-procedure, he experienced neurological deterioration and loss of consciousness with elevated homocysteine levels (43 mmol/L). Nitrous oxide-induced methionine synthase inhibition may precipitate transient ischaemic events in genetically susceptible patients.

D3.title: From neural propagation to conscious experience: A geometro-diffusion theory of consciousness
D3.abstract: Theories of consciousness frequently emphasize integration, differentiation, recurrent processing, or global availability, but the mathematical organization connecting neural propagation with subjective experience remains unclear. We introduce the Geometro-Diffusion Theory (GDT), in which diffusion-like dynamics on a structured substrate induces an intrinsic relational geometry. We introduce the Diffusion-Based Machine (DBM) as an operational model designed to distinguish information obtained from a single realized activity pattern from invariant information encoded across the family of possible dynamical responses. We show that independent diffusion realizations generate a Euclidean embedding whose Gram matrix is the diffusion kernel. This construction reveals metric relations, equivalence classes, symmetries, and globally organized routes that may remain inaccessible from an individual realization. To quantify this distinction, we define a partition gap comparing observational and geometric classifications and a normalized signature difference measuring their respective temporal differentiation. The central hypothesis is that conscious experience requires an intrinsic mechanism capable of accessing, integrating, and recursively using invariants of a sufficiently rich diffusion-induced geometry. Diffusion or geometry alone is therefore insufficient. We discuss how recurrent neural interactions, continuous activity, population integration, feedback, and plasticity could implement the required geometric access without explicit mathematical computation. The framework is summarized by six principles specifying the substrate, propagation dynamics, emergence and timescale of geometry, intrinsic decoding, and recursive integration. GDT provides operational quantities that can be examined using perturbational neural data across wakefulness, sleep, anesthesia, and disorders of consciousness.

D3.title: Biomarkers in Patients With Acute Ischaemic Stroke Undergoing Thrombectomy Compared With Controls: A Pilot Study
D3.abstract: Detection of cerebral ischaemia is challenging in patients who are anaesthetised, sedated or have reduced levels of consciousness, as neurological examination is difficult or even impossible to assess. Furthermore, as some patients cannot be transported for radiology, for example during surgery, a reliable blood biomarker for detecting acute cerebral events would be of considerable clinical value. We aimed to compare levels of brain injury biomarkers glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), neurofilament light chain (NfL), and total tau (tau) in patients with acute ischaemic stroke (AIS) undergoing endovascular thrombectomy under general anaesthesia or sedation to controls undergoing non-cerebral surgery under general anaesthesia. These biomarkers were chosen because previous studies have demonstrated their potential as blood biomarkers of acute cerebral injury and ischaemic stroke. In this prospective, observational pilot study, conducted at the Sahlgrenska University Hospital, Gothenburg, Sweden, between 2021 and 2024, GFAP, NfL, and tau were analysed using the Simoa Neurology 4-plex assay, before thrombectomy or surgery and at 2- and 24 h thereafter. Blood samples from 21 patients with AIS and 19 controls were analysed. GFAP concentrations in patients with AIS increased significantly from baseline to 24 h (median 301.0 → 1443.0 pg/mL; p = 0.001) and were higher than in controls at all time points (p < 0.01). In the controls there was no significant increase in GFAP from baseline to 24 h (p = 0.449). NfL and tau increased significantly in patients with AIS (p = 0.001 and 0.002) but also in the controls (p = 0.001 and 0.047). GFAP and NfL concentrations were higher in patients with acute ischaemic stroke than in surgical controls at all sampling time points, whereas tau differed only after 24 h. Unlike NfL and tau, GFAP did not increase significantly in controls, suggesting that it may be less influenced by anaesthesia and surgery. These findings support further evaluation of GFAP as a potential biomarker of acute cerebral injury in perioperative and critical care settings. A biomarker of ischaemic cerebral injury could be attractive to support treatments to protect brain health during anaesthesia and surgery. In a pilot study, glial fibrillary acidic protein emerged as a potential candidate as it was increased in patients undergoing endovascular thrombectomy for large-vessel ischaemic stroke compared to anaesthetised patients undergoing non-cerebral surgery. D3.title: Longitudinal associations between appearance-related social media consciousness and sleep in U.S. middle schoolers
D3.journal: Journal of research on adolescence : the official journal of the Society for Research on Adolescence
D3.abstract: Social media use has been linked to poorer sleep outcomes in adolescents, yet the mechanisms underlying this association remain unclear. Appearance-related social media consciousness (ASMC)-a preoccupation with one's appearance online-could relate to offline behaviors, including sleep. This study examined the association between ASMC and various sleep behaviors using a parallel mediation structural equation model. Participants were 1158 U.S. 8th-grade students (Mage = 13.14, 52% girls, 36% Hispanic/Latine, 37% qualified for free or reduced-price lunch) surveyed at two points across an academic year. Higher ASMC was indirectly associated with poorer sleep quality, increased sleep disturbances, and longer sleep onset latency through greater compulsive nighttime social media use. Additionally, higher ASMC was indirectly associated with earlier sleep onset times through longer morning routine durations. Findings suggest that appearance-related experiences on social media have implications for adolescent sleep health and provide preliminary support for some pathways through which its effects may occur.

D3.title: The EEG multi-scale brain network and high-order synergy changes in disorders of consciousness during general anesthesia
D3.abstract: Brain network alterations during general anesthesia (GA) have been extensively investigated in individuals with intact consciousness. However, network dynamics in patients with disorders of consciousness (DoC) under anesthetic perturbation remain poorly understood. We recorded electroencephalogram (EEG) signals from 33 DoC patients (16 UWS and 17 MCS) during GA across three states (DoC-Resting, DoC-MOSSA, and DoC-Recovery). A multi-scale brain network framework was proposed. Low-order network characteristics were assessed using unbiased minimum spanning tree (MST) and directed phase lag index (dPLI), while high-order organization was evaluated using topological data analysis (TDA) and high-order mutual information (HO-MI). UWS patients exhibited a fragmented, line-like topological backbone with lower leaf fraction (p < 0.05) and tree hierarchy (p < 0.05) than MCS patients. dPLI analysis revealed impaired prefrontal top-down directional communication in UWS patients, whereas MCS patients showed transient disruption and recovery of frontoparietal directional organization during anesthesia. Under anesthesia, TDA revealed reduced H1 maximum Betti number in UWS patients (p < 0.01), indicating impaired topological resilience, while MCS patients showed relatively preserved network organization. Furthermore, HO-MI analysis showed increased total correlation with redundant information processing in UWS patients during anesthesia, whereas MCS patients restored synergistic information integration within the central-parietal network during recovery. GA reveals distinct scale-dependent network alterations between MCS and UWS patients. Persistent impairment of directed communication and high-order synergistic integration characterizes disrupted network organization in UWS. The proposed multi-scale EEG framework integrating MST, dPLI, TDA, and HO-MI provides candidate network biomarkers for perioperative consciousness monitoring and assessment in DoC patients. D3.title: Effect of Intraoperative Hemispheric Synchronized Sounds on Depth of Anesthesia and Postoperative Pain in Children Undergoing Infraumbilical Surgery: A Double-Blinded Randomized Controlled Trial
D3.abstract: Binaural beats have been shown to have sedative effects in adults. Our study aimed to evaluate the effect of hemispheric synchronized sounds on depth of anesthesia primarily and postoperative pain relief in children. This study aimed to evaluate the effect of Intraoperative hemispheric synchronized sounds on depth of anesthesia in children undergoing infraumbilical surgeries receiving caudal epidural block along with general anesthesia. We also determined postoperative pain and analgesic requirement. A double blinded randomized controlled trial was conducted at a tertiary care hospital in India on 60 children between the ages of 6 months to 7 years planned for elective infraumbilical surgery under general anesthesia with caudal epidural block. The study subjects were allocated into two equal groups, Group-S (headphones applied, blank file played) and Group-H (headphones applied, hemispheric synchronized sounds played). Bispectral index (BIS) values were recorded every 5 min till the end of the procedure; duration of sound file played and FLACC score at 60 min and 24 h after surgery were also recorded. The study conducted in the pediatric population had a mean age of 4.02 ± 2.08 in group H and 4.77 ± 2.16 in group S. Both groups had comparable gender distribution (66.6% males in group H and 76.6% males in group S). The mean ± SD Intraoperative BIS values were 47.18 ± 9.77 in Group H and 54.32 ± 6.15 in group S (p = 0.001). The median (IQR) postoperative FLACC score at 60 min in group S was 0 (0-1) and group H was 0 (0-1) (p = 0.539). The postoperative FLACC score at 24 h was 0 in both groups. In our study, we observed that these sounds deepened the plane of anesthesia and had no evidence of a statistically significant difference in postoperative pain scores. We conclude that they may be used as part of a multimodal therapy to reduce the requirement of pharmacological anesthetic agents thereby alleviating their short-term and long-term effects. D3.title: Effects of Esketamine on Postoperative Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale Scores in Patients Undergoing Laparoscopic Radical Resection for Colorectal Cancer
D3.journal: Journal of investigative surgery : the official journal of the Academy of Surgical Research
D3.abstract: To investigate the effects of intravenous esketamine on postoperative Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS) scores in patients undergoing laparoscopic radical resection for colorectal cancer. In this prospective, randomized, placebo-controlled study, adult patients for elective laparoscopic radical resection were randomly assigned (1:1) to a control group (group C) or an esketamine group (group PE). Group C received conventional general anesthesia and patient-controlled intravenous analgesia (PCIA). In group PE, esketamine 0.5 mg/kg was injected during induction of anesthesia, with esketamine 1 mg/kg added to PCIA. Primary outcome was HADS score on postoperative day 1. Secondary outcomes included HADS scores on postoperative days 3 and 7, sleep quality scores, postoperative level of consciousness, complication rate, length of hospital stay, 24 h inflammatory factors, and satisfaction scores. Group PE showed significantly lower HADS-A and HADS-D scores on postoperative days 1 and 3 , reduced 24 h interleukin-6 (IL-6) leveland higher patient satisfaction compared with group C (all p < 0.05). Esketamine given during induction and in PCIA reduced early-stage postoperative HADS scores and improved patient satisfaction in colorectal cancer patients.
